1.

The petitioner, who is the victim in the present case, has preferred this revision petition assailing
the order dated 04.08.2009 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge (Fast Track) No.1,
Bikaner in Sessions Case No.108/2008, whereby the learned trial court discharged the respondent
for the offence under Section 376 Ipc and remanded the matter to the Court of the Chief Judicial
Magistrate for conducting the trial only for the offences under Sections 384 and 420 Ipc.
2.

The facts, briefly stated, are that the petitioner-complainant filed a private complaint on 13.12.2007 before the Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, Jaipur, inter alia alleging that she had been [2025:RJ-JD:31317] (2 of 7) [CRLR-1169/2009] married to Dr. Sandeep Kumar for nearly 15 years.

However, during the course of time, the accused Surendra Kumar allegedly entered her life,
exerted pressure and threats, and induced her to transfer her property and valuables in his name.

sentences.text: The complainant further alleged that the accused sexually assaulted her in April 2005 at Jaipur and subjected her to financial and physical exploitation.
2.1 This is the second round of litigation.

Initially, charges were framed against the accused under Sections 376, 384, and 420 IPC, which came to be challenged before this Court by the accused by way of S.B. Criminal Revision Petition No.1116/2008, assailing the order dated 03.10.2008 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge (Fast Track) No.1, Bikaner.

entities.text: Additional Sessions Judge (Fast Track) No.1, Bikaner
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: 2.2 This Court, vide order dated 06.03.2009, set aside the charge to the extent of Section 376 IPC and remanded the matter to the learned trial court for reconsideration in accordance with law.
Upon fresh consideration, the trial court, after affording adequate opportunity to both sides, discharged the accused of the offence under Section 376 IPC.

Since the charges under Sections 384 and 420 IPC were already framed and were triable by the Magistrate, the matter was remitted to the Court of the Chief Judicial Magistrate, which aggrieved the petitioner.
2.3 Upon remand, both parties were afforded an opportunity of hearing and the record was re-evaluated afresh.

It emerged from the complainant's own statement as well as other evidence that she had entered into marriage with the accused in 2004, after [2025:RJ-JD:31317] (3 of 7) [CRLR-1169/2009] being abandoned by her husband Dr. Sandeep Kumar.
From 2004 to 2007, she and the accused cohabited in Jaipur and Bikaner, ran a joint business, and were known in society as husband and wife.
The complainant admitted to having conceived twice during this period, one pregnancy being medically terminated at DCM Nursing Home, Jaipur, on 22.06.2006.

This lends credence to the existence of a prolonged,
consensual relationship.

2.4 The record is further fortified by the testimonies of independent witnesses including Anisha,
Neelam Chaudhary, Naresh Kumar, Nitin Kumar, Banwari Lal, Amitabh and Gopal Chaudhary, who consistently stated that the complainant and the accused jointly resided and operated a shop and were socially accepted as a couple.

None of these witnesses observed any element of coercion, deceit,
or disharmony during their cohabitation.

2.5 Additionally, the complainant's estranged husband, Dr. Sandeep Kumar, testified that she had deserted the matrimonial home in 1993 after the birth of their third child and had since been in a live-in relationship with Surendra Kumar.
He specifically stated that she moved to Jaipur with the accused and even made efforts to lay claim to his (Dr. Sandeep's) property.
3. I have heard the learned counsel for the parties at length and perused the entire record of the case with due care and circumspection.

4. It is pertinent to note that the Coordinate Bench of this Court in its earlier order dated 06.03.2009 had given a categorical [2025:RJ-JD:31317] (4 of 7) [CRLR-1169/2009] finding that the free consent and voluntary submission of a major married woman would not fall within the ambit of Section 375 IPC.
For ready reference, the relevant portion of the said order is reproduced herein below:

sentences.text: "As per record it is not the case of the prosecution that the consent had been obtained by fraud or misrepresentation.
The complainant has stated that she married with the accused-petitioner.
Twice she conceived out of her relationship with the accused-petitioner.

Thus, she herself has submitted for sexual intercourse but the learned trial court has not properly considered the statements of the complainant and in a routine manner ordered to frame charge under Section 376 I.P.C., that liable to be quashed."
The Coordinate Bench of this Court had already quashed the charge under Section 376 IPC.
Upon remand, the learned trial court, after due application of mind, also found no justification to proceed under Section 376 IPC and accordingly discharged the accused.
5. This Court is of the view that the trial court has rightly appreciated the facts and legal position.

In light of the judgment rendered by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Prashant Bharti v. State (NCT of Delhi), reported in (2013) 9 SCC 293, it has been observed:
"16.

entities.text: Prashant Bharti v. State (NCT of Delhi), reported in (2013) 9 SCC 293
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The factual position narrated above would enable us to draw some positive inferences on the assertion made by the complainant/prosecutrix-against the Appellant-accused (in the supplementary statement dated 21.2.2007).
It is relevant to notice, that she had alleged, that she was induced into a physical relationship by Prashant Bharti, on the assurance that he would marry her.
Obviously, an inducement for marriage is understandable if the same is made to an unmarried person.
The judgment and decree dated 23.9.2008 reveals, that the complainant/prosecutrix was married to Lalji Porwal on 14.6.2003.

It also reveals,
that the aforesaid marriage subsisted till 23.9.2008, when the two divorced one another by mutual consent under [2025:RJ-JD:31317] (5 of 7) [CRLR-1169/2009]
Section 13B of the Hindu Marriage Act.

In her supplementary statement dated 21.2.2007, the complainant/prosecutrix accused Prashant Bhati of having had physical relations with her on 23.12.2006, 25.12.2006 and 1.1.2007 at his residence,
on the basis of a false promise to marry her.

It is apparent from irrefutable evidence,
that during the dates under reference and for a period of more than one year and eight months thereafter, she had remained married to Lalji Porwal.

In such a fact situation, the assertion made by the complainant/prosecutrix, that the Appellant-accused had physical relations with her, on the assurance that he would marry her, is per se false and as such, unacceptable.

She, more than anybody else,
was clearly aware of the fact that she had a subsisting valid marriage with Lalji Porwal.
Accordingly, there was no question of anyone being in a position to induce her into a physical relationship under an assurance of marriage.

If the judgment and decree dated 23.9.2008 produced before us by the complainant/prosecutrix herself is taken into consideration alongwith the factual position depicted in the supplementary statement dated 21.2.2007,-it would clearly emerge, that the complainant/prosecutrix was in a relationship of adultery on 23.12.2006, 25.12.2006 and 1.1.2007 with the Appellant-accused, while she was validly married to her previous husband Lalji Porwal.

In the aforesaid view of the matter, we are satisfied Swati Swami vs State And Anr. (2025:Rj-Jd:31317) on 10 July, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/49379189/
3 that the assertion made by the complainant/prosecutrix, that she was induced to a physical relationship by Prashant Bharti, the Appellant-accused, on the basis of a promise to marry her, stands irrefutably falsified."

entities.text: Swati Swami vs State And Anr. (2025:Rj-Jd:31317)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: From bare perusal of the case referred supra, it would be absurd to hold that a married woman, who is already in a subsisting matrimonial relationship, can be said to have been lured into a physical relationship on the pretext of marriage.

Such allegations, on the face of it, do not satisfy the ingredients of Section 375 IPC.
6.
The facts of the present case are squarely covered by the ratio laid down in Prashant Bharti (supra).

The allegations made [2025:RJ-JD:31317] (6 of 7) [CRLR-1169/2009] by the petitioner,
even if taken at their face value, do not constitute the offence under Section 376 IPC.
Thus, the impugned order does not suffer from any infirmity warranting interference by this Court.
The charge under Section 376 IPC was rightly set aside earlier, and the subsequent discharge is in consonance with law and binding precedent.
7. The learned trial court, in its detailed and reasoned judgment, concluded that no prima facie case was made out under Section 376 IPC.

The existence of a long-standing domestic relationship, the complainant's acknowledgment of marriage, her pregnancy and medical records, and the absence of contemporaneous complaints of coercion or fraud, all go to undermine the foundational basis of the allegations.
8. This Court finds no perversity or misapplication of law in the reasoning adopted by the trial court.
On the contrary, the conclusions are well-supported by the factual matrix and legally tenable.

9. It is now a well-established principle of criminal jurisprudence that an accused is presumed innocent until proven guilty, and such presumption attains greater force once the accused is discharged by a competent court.

The Revisional or Appellate Court must exercise caution and restraint in interfering with an order of discharge unless it is shown that the trial court's observations are manifestly erroneous, perverse, or vitiated by a gross misreading of material and therefore, either the order of discharge is illegal, not proper or not found correct after having [2025:RJ-JD:31317] (7 of 7) [CRLR-1169/2009] done an examination in revisional jurisdiction.
Applying the above principles to the case at hand, this Court is of the considered view that the learned trial court's decision to discharge the respondent- accused is neither legally flawed nor factually infirm.
The observations and conclusion are in consonance with the material on record and the applicable legal standards.
10. Accordingly, the Criminal Revision Petition stands dismissed being devoid of merit.

The judgment dated 04.08.2009, passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge (Fast Track) No.1,
Bikaner in Sessions Case No.108/2008 (State vs. Surendra Kumar), is upheld and affirmed.
